title: Song of Solomon 8:1–7
context: The Beloved wishes she could show her love openly and bring him to her mother’s house, and repeats the embrace and the charge not to awaken love until it so desires (cf. 2:6–7; 3:5). The Friends ask who comes up from the wilderness, and the Beloved asks to be set as a seal on his heart, for love is strong as death and many waters cannot quench it. Both traditions read 8:6–7 as shared ground on the strength and faithfulness of love, whether read of marriage or of God’s love for his people, and its images are hedged. Speaker names (Lover, Beloved, Friends, Brothers) follow the WEB headings, which are interpretive and are not part of the Hebrew text.

verses.text: Oh that you were like my brother, who nursed from the breasts of my mother! If I found you outside, I would kiss you; yes, and no one would despise me.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Beloved says, “Oh that you were like my brother... If I found you outside, I would kiss you; yes, and no one would despise me.” Arminian readers note her wish that their love could be openly acknowledged.

The verse reflects social customs of the time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a longing for love to be honored publicly.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a desire for love that is open and honorable, and allegorical readers see a longing for nearness to God.

verses.text: I would lead you, bringing you into the house of my mother, who would instruct me. I would have you drink spiced wine, of the juice of my pomegranate.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I would lead you, bringing you into the house of my mother, who would instruct me.” Arminian readers note the echo of 3:4, where she brings him into her mother’s house.

The home is a place of welcome and family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see love set within family and home.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as love welcomed into a family setting, and they read the imagery of spiced wine with restraint as hospitality and joy.

verses.text: His left hand would be under my head. His right hand would embrace me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“His left hand would be under my head. His right hand would embrace me.” Arminian readers note that this repeats 2:6, where the verbs read “is” and “embraces.”

The image is one of rest and security.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a picture of protective care.

Shared ground: both traditions read the embrace as security in love, and allegorical readers in both see the believer resting in God’s care (cf. Deut 33:27).

verses.text: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, that you not stir up, nor awaken love, until it so desires.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Beloved charges the daughters of Jerusalem “that you not stir up, nor awaken love, until it so desires.” Arminian readers note that the charge repeats 2:7 and 3:5, here without the mention of roes and hinds.

Love is not to be rushed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see wisdom about the right time for love.

Shared ground: both traditions see the repeated charge as counsel on patience and purity, and they do not harmonize the slight differences in wording.

verses.text: Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved? Under the apple tree I awakened you. There your mother conceived you. There she was in labor and bore you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Friends ask, “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved?” Arminian readers note that the question resembles 3:6.

The Beloved then speaks of the apple tree and of his mother’s labor, images whose exact meaning is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a picture of dependence and trust. Allegorical readers have seen the church coming up from the wilderness leaning on Christ, as a reading.

Shared ground: both traditions hedge the images and read the verse as love rooted in shared history.

verses.text: Set me as a seal on your heart, as a seal on your arm; for love is strong as death. Jealousy is as cruel as Sheol. Its flashes are flashes of fire, a very flame of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Set me as a seal on your heart, as a seal on your arm; for love is strong as death.” Arminian readers note that a seal could mark identity and belonging (cf. Gen 38:18; Hag 2:23).

WEB ends the verse with “a very flame of the LORD”; whether the divine name is intended or the phrase is an intensive is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see love that is exclusive and enduring. Allegorical readers in both traditions hear God’s faithful love, which Christians often connect with Romans 8:38–39.

Shared ground: both traditions read 8:6 as praise of committed love, without making it a contrast.

verses.text: Many waters can’t quench love, neither can floods drown it. If a man would give all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Many waters can’t quench love, neither can floods drown it.” Arminian readers note that love cannot be overcome by forces that threaten it.

“If a man would give all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned”: love cannot be bought.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see love as a gift that cannot be purchased.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as praise of faithful love, whether between spouses or between God and his people, and allegorical readers see God’s love that cannot be earned or defeated.
